questions.question: Which sentence emphasizes the LOCATION of the bank?
choices: The BANK is on Main Street
The bank is on MAIN Street
The bank is on Main STREET
The BANK is on Main STREET
questions.explanation: Primary stress on BANK indicates it's the location you're identifying—the bank building itself. Main Street is the subordinate information.

questions.question: Listen to the phrase 'I didn't say SHE stole my money.' Which word does the stress challenge?
choices: Emphasizing 'SHE' questions if she was the thief
Emphasizing 'I' questions who made the claim
Emphasizing 'my' indicates emotional ownership
Emphasizing 'money' questions the value
questions.explanation: The stress pattern in 'I didn't say SHE stole' uses contrastive emphasis on SHE to imply someone else may have done it—it's questioning the identity of the thief.

questions.question: How does stress change the meaning: 'I can PRESENT this idea' vs. 'I CAN present this idea'?
choices: First emphasizes the presentation act, second emphasizes ability
First emphasizes ability, second emphasizes the act
No difference—both mean the same thing
First is polite, second is rude
questions.explanation: Stress on CAN emphasizes your ability or permission to present. Stress on PRESENT emphasizes the action itself. Word choice of stress reveals what you want to highlight.

questions.question: Which stress pattern suggests disagreement or contrast?
choices: Even stress across all words
Primary stress on the first word
Placing unexpected stress on typically unstressed words
Stress only at the end of the sentence
questions.explanation: Contrastive stress—moving emphasis to unexpected syllables—signals disagreement or introduces a contrasting point. 'I didn't say SHE stole it' uses this pattern to contradict an assumption.

questions.question: In 'Can you PRESENT this?' the stress on PRESENT most likely indicates:
choices: A question about physical ability
Doubt or disbelief about the capability
Request for a specific action
Polite disagreement
questions.explanation: Stress on the action verb (PRESENT) in a question form requests or emphasizes that specific action. It clarifies you want them to do the presentation, not something else.

questions.question: How does stress shift meaning: 'That's not MY responsibility' vs. 'That's MY responsibility'?
choices: First denies responsibility, second accepts it
Both mean the same thing
First is emphatic acceptance, second is denial
Stress has no effect on meaning here
questions.explanation: Stress on MY in 'not MY responsibility' contrastively emphasizes that it belongs to someone else. In 'That's MY responsibility,' stress affirms ownership.

questions.question: Which pattern indicates new or surprising information in speech?
choices: Reduced stress throughout
Stress on already-known or expected information
Stress on new, unexpected, or contrastive elements
Random stress placement
questions.explanation: In English, speakers stress new information (focus) and de-stress given/known information. 'The BANK is on Main Street' stresses bank if new; 'The bank is on Main STREET' if the location detail is new.

questions.question: In conversation, if someone asks 'Did you finish the report?' and you respond 'I FINISHED the report,' what are you emphasizing?
choices: That you are capable of finishing things
That you completed the action (but perhaps not what comes next)
That the report exists
Disagreement with the question
questions.explanation: Stress on FINISHED emphasizes the completed action itself. It confirms you did finish—the verb is the focus—suggesting perhaps the next step is unclear.

questions.question: What does primary stress on the first word of a phrase typically signal?
choices: The most important information in context
An error in pronunciation
A question rather than a statement
Emphasis on the entire phrase equally
questions.explanation: Stress position reveals information focus. Stress on the first word highlights the beginning element as central to meaning—often used to introduce or emphasize the subject.

questions.question: How do you distinguish emphasis from normal word stress in English?
choices: Emphasis is always louder, normal stress is always quieter
Emphasis moves stress away from typical syllables; normal stress follows dictionary patterns
There is no difference—they are the same
Emphasis uses higher pitch, normal stress uses lower pitch only
questions.explanation: Normal word stress follows predictable patterns (e.g., PREsent as noun, preSENT as verb). Emphasis moves stress to unexpected syllables or words to create meaning (e.g., 'I didn't say SHE stole it').
